name: Pump fracturing stages on one well
summary: A 24-hour frac crew pumps every stage of one horizontal well to the treatment design, usually alternating with a second well on the same pad while the producer's wireline crew perforates the next stage (zipper fracturing). The treater calls rate and sand changes from the data van, pump, blender and sand operators run the equipment, and the field supervisor runs the location and deals with the customer's wellsite supervisor. Time is lost between stages waiting on wireline, and whenever a pump fails, a stage screens out, sand, water or fuel run short, or weather stops work, the whole fleet and crew stand by. Volumes pumped, fuel and pump hours are then re-keyed from the data van and paper sheets into the field ticket.

baseline.org_archetype: A TSX-listed Canadian pressure pumping company with six to eight 24-hour frac crews working for producers in Alberta and northeast BC, run from district bases with a Calgary head office.
baseline.notes: Modelled on the organisation file oilfield-services-co (composite based on Trican and STEP Canada). 2020 was a deep downturn and sits at the low end of volume ranges.

unit_of_work: one well fractured (all stages of one horizontal well)
trigger: The rig-up and pressure test record for the pad is signed off and the customer's wellsite supervisor releases the first well for fracturing.
end_state: The last stage of the well is pumped, volumes are reconciled and entered for the field ticket, data files are exported, and the customer is told the well is complete (and, for the last well, that the pad is complete).

volume.seasonality: Highest from January to mid-March on frozen ground, lowest in April and May during spring break-up road bans, steady from June to December; 2020 was far below the other years.

surge.cause: Winter completion peak while frozen ground allows access to muskeg leases (January to mid-March)

evidence.note: Same surge as the organisation file's process map entry (crews fully booked January to mid-March); the multiplier is an estimate from quarterly proppant swings of 260,000-479,000 tonnes in the organisation file.

Organisation file driver frac-wells (6-7 active crews at about 7-8 wells per crew-month). Cross-check: about 1.34-1.36 million tonnes of proppant a year in the organisation file over about 600 wells gives about 2,250 tonnes a well, roughly two operating days at the 1,040 tonnes per operating day STEP Canada reported for 2021.
Organisation file headcount 24 (one per shift rotation for each 24-hour crew). About 60% of field time on pumping; the rest on rig-up, rig-down, moves and paperwork (estimate).
Organisation file headcount 24. About 58% of time on pumping (estimate); the rest on rig-up checks, post-job reports and NPT handling.
Organisation file headcount 26; about 55% of time on stage acquisition (estimate).

Organisation file headcount 316 (about 15 per shift rotation per crew). About 60% of time on pumping and between-stage maintenance; the rest on rig-up, rig-down, driving units between pads and yard work (estimate). Duties from the alis profile.
Organisation file headcount 45 (about two per shift); about 55% of time on pumping (estimate).
Organisation file headcount 30; about 45% of time feeding proppant during pumping, the rest on receiving trucks and inventory (documented in the onsite proppant workflow).

systems.name: Data van acquisition and treatment monitoring system
Electronic field ticketing on tablets, linked to the ERP price book
Email, Microsoft Teams and mobile phones
HSE incident, hazard assessment and audit system
Maintenance work order and equipment history module

resources.name: Crewed hydraulic fracturing fleet (pumps, blender, data van, sand and chemical units, treating iron)
Frac pump unit (2,500 to 3,000 HHP, trailer mounted)
Wellsite proppant storage and conveyor units

steps.name: Load the pump schedule into the data van
steps.description: The data van technician opens the treatment design for the well and builds the stage-by-stage pump schedule in the acquisition software: fluid volumes, rates, proppant ramps by mesh and chemical loadings. They set alarm limits for treating pressure and check sensor zeroes on the treating line.

error.defect_description: A ramp, volume or alarm limit is keyed wrongly from the design.

evidence.note: Common practice for data-van acquisition; per-well time is an estimate.

steps.name: Agree the stage plan with the customer's wellsite supervisor
steps.description: The treater walks the customer's wellsite supervisor (company man) through the pump schedule, stage order across the pad wells and any changes from the design, such as a lower maximum pressure or a different proppant ramp. Both initial the schedule; changes later in the well also need the supervisor's agreement.

control.basis: Customer completion program and master service agreement: deviations from the treatment design need the wellsite supervisor's approval

evidence.note: Customer approval of design changes is standard in WCSB frac programs; time estimated.

steps.name: Lead the shift safety meeting
steps.description: At each shift change the field supervisor holds the safety meeting at the data van: the day's stages, pressure limits, red-zone rules around the treating iron, hazards on the field level hazard assessment and who is the designated spotter. The supervisor records attendance and signs the hazard assessment. Time shown is this well's share of the meetings on the pad.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 2 hazard assessment and company pre-job safety meeting at every shift change on a pressure pumping location

evidence.note: Shift safety meetings are standard practice on frac locations; the per-well share assumes about four shift changes per well and three wells per pad.

steps.name: Crew attends the meeting and walks the iron
steps.description: Pump, blender and sand operators on the incoming shift attend the meeting, then walk the treating iron, check valve positions and look for leaks or loose restraints before pressure comes back on. Each operator signs the hazard assessment.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 2 hazard assessment and company pre-job safety meeting at every shift change on a pressure pumping location

evidence.note: Crew of about 13 pump operators per shift from the organisation file headcount (316 over 7 crews and 3 rotations).

steps.name: Wireline perforates and hands the well back
steps.description: The producer's wireline crew pumps down a plug and perforating guns, sets the plug, fires the guns and pulls out, then tells the treater the well is ready. With zipper fracturing most of this runs while the other well on the pad is being pumped; the time shown is the dead time this well adds: well swaps and stages where wireline is not ready when the pumps are.

evidence.note: Wireline plug-and-perf takes 2-3 hours (up to 5) between stages on a single well and about 15 minutes of dead time with zipper fracturing (JPT). Per-well dead time assumes about 28 stages at 15-40 minutes.

steps.name: Grease valves and check fluid ends during wireline runs
steps.description: While wireline works, a few pump operators grease the pump valves and plug valves, check fluid ends for washed seats and leaks, top up oil and fuel and swap any pump flagged by the treater. This maintenance between stages decides how many pumping hours the fleet gets in a day.

error.defect_description: A worn valve or seat is missed and fails during the next stage.

evidence.note: Managing maintenance schedules raised available pumping hours per day (STEP case study); minutes per well are an estimate.

steps.name: Confirm the handover and line up the well
steps.description: Before each stage the treater confirms with wireline and the wellsite supervisor that the guns fired and the plug is set, checks the wellhead valve positions on the frac stack for the right well, and equalises pressure before opening. Time is about five minutes per stage summed over the well.

error.defect_description: A valve is left in the wrong position on the zipper manifold.

control.basis: Company and IRP 24 surface operations practice: valve line-up and pressure equalisation check before opening a well to the pumps

evidence.note: Stage-by-stage line-up checks are standard on zipper pads; time estimated.

steps.name: Pump the stages to the design
steps.description: Pump operators bring the pumps up to rate on the treater's call and run them from the pump control cab through pad, proppant ramps and flush on every stage, watching engine and transmission readings. Time shown is total pumping time for the well, about 28 stages of 60 to 90 minutes.

error.defect_description: A pump is run past its limits and fails later.

evidence.note: About 1,040 tonnes pumped per operating day in Canada (STEP 2021) and 14-19 pumping hours a day (STEP case study) imply about 30-40 pumping hours for a 2,250-tonne well.

steps.name: Mix fluid and add chemicals on the blender
steps.description: The blender operator runs the blender tub and liquid additive pumps, holding friction reducer, crosslinker, breaker and biocide rates to the schedule and keeping tub level steady. They watch chemical tote levels and call for a tote change before one runs dry.

error.defect_description: A chemical rate drifts from the schedule for part of a stage.

evidence.note: Two blender operators per shift from organisation file headcount (45 over 21 shift rotations).

steps.name: Feed proppant from wellsite storage to the blender
steps.description: The sand operator runs the conveyors from the storage units to the blender, switching mesh sizes at the stage changes the treater calls and keeping the blender hopper full during the ramps. They watch storage levels and warn the treater when a mesh is running low.

error.defect_description: The wrong mesh is fed for part of a stage.

evidence.note: Storage units feed the blender directly (Source Energy Sahara page); one sand operator per shift from organisation file headcount.

steps.name: Watch pressures and call rate and sand changes
steps.description: The treater watches treating pressure, rate and proppant concentration on the data van screens, compares them with the design and calls changes: cut the ramp if net pressure climbs, drop rate, extend the pad or go to flush early. They decide on the spot when a pressure trend signals a screen-out.

control.basis: Maximum allowable treating pressure and pressure relief settings from the treatment design and the producer's wellhead rating

evidence.note: Treater role as described in the organisation file; continuous presence during pumping.

steps.name: Record stage data and stage summaries
steps.description: The data van technician keeps acquisition running, marks stage start and end, notes events such as rate cuts or pump trips and prints or emails a one-page stage summary (volumes, average and maximum pressure, proppant by mesh) after each stage for the wellsite supervisor.

error.defect_description: A stage boundary or event is marked wrongly in the record.

evidence.note: Common data-van practice; continuous presence during pumping.

steps.name: Run the location during pumping
steps.description: The field supervisor coordinates everything around the pumps: sand and fuel trucks, wireline timing, water transfer, crew breaks, and the customer's questions. When something stops pumping they decide with the treater what to do next and who to call.

next.condition: a stage screens out or pressures out
a pump or blender component fails
pumping stops for sand, water, fuel or wireline
an incident, spill or offset-well communication

evidence.note: Branch shares are estimates that give about 0.4 stoppages per well (about 19 a month), against 10-45 non-productive time events a month in the organisation file. STEP reported extended client-location delays from well conditions and weather in Q4 2021.

steps.name: Cut sand and flush after a screen-out
steps.description: When treating pressure climbs fast and the well stops taking proppant, the treater cuts sand, calls a flush and, if pressure reaches the limit, shuts the pumps down. They tell the wellsite supervisor and the field supervisor and start the screen-out procedure.

control.basis: Maximum allowable treating pressure and pressure relief settings from the treatment design

evidence.note: Typical screen-out response; frequency of 10% of wells is an estimate.

steps.name: Stand by while the well is flowed back or cleaned out
steps.description: The crew waits while the well is flowed back to clear sand from the perforations, or while the customer brings in coiled tubing to clean out. The supervisor keeps the crew busy on maintenance and tracks the stop and start times. The screen-out workflow covers the decisions made during this time.

evidence.note: Flowback takes hours; a coiled tubing cleanout can take one to two days including mobilisation (estimate).

steps.name: Isolate and swap a failed pump
steps.description: When a pump trips or a fluid end washes out, operators isolate it with the plug valves, bleed it off and either repair it on location or swap in the standby pump. Pumping often continues at lower rate on the other pumps; a blender or manifold failure stops the stage.

error.defect_description: Pressure is not fully bled before the pump is opened.

control.basis: Company energy isolation and bleed-off procedure for high-pressure treating iron (Alberta OHS Code hazardous energy control)

evidence.note: About 0.2 pump or blender failures per well is an estimate consistent with 20-30 pumps run hard for 30-40 hours.

steps.name: Stand by for sand, water, fuel or wireline
steps.description: Pumping stops because a mesh has run out in storage, the water transfer cannot keep up, fuel is late or wireline has a misfire or stuck tool. The supervisor chases the logistics coordinator, the water contractor or the wellsite supervisor and logs the standby time.

evidence.note: Delay lengths estimated; causes as listed in the organisation file process description.

steps.name: Hold for weather
steps.description: Extreme cold freezes lines and water, lightning or high winds stop work around the iron, or a storm stops trucks reaching the pad. The supervisor shuts down, keeps lines circulating or heated where possible and restarts when conditions allow.

control.basis: Company cold weather and lightning stop-work rules

evidence.note: STEP reported late-December 2021 weather delays and January 2022 extreme cold delays in Canada; durations estimated.

steps.name: Stop and report an incident, spill or offset-well communication
steps.description: Pumping stops for an injury, a fluid release at surface or a pressure response at an offset well reported by the customer. The supervisor makes the site safe, calls the customer and the HSE advisor, and starts the incident or spill report; the customer files any Directive 083 communication-event report with the AER.

control.basis: AER Directive 083 communication-event reporting (licensee) and Alberta OHS incident reporting

evidence.note: Directive 083 reporting channels for offset-well communication events and surface releases (AER page); frequency estimated.

steps.name: Customer witness signs the stage summaries
steps.description: The customer's wellsite supervisor reads the stage summaries, compares proppant placed with the design and initials them, or notes stages that were cut short. These signed sheets back up the field ticket later.

evidence.note: Common practice; time estimated.

steps.name: Switch to backup recording and raise an IT ticket
steps.description: If the acquisition computer, a sensor or the satellite link fails, the data technician switches to the backup recorder or paper logging so pumping can continue, and raises a ticket with IT for the data van.

error.defect_description: Part of a stage is recorded by hand with gaps.

evidence.note: Estimate.

steps.name: Log the stoppage and send an NPT report
steps.description: The supervisor writes down when pumping stopped and restarted, the cause, the units affected and who they think is responsible, and sends it to the operations manager and the customer. This opens the non-productive time workflow.

error.defect_description: Stop and start times or cause are recorded loosely.

evidence.note: Estimate.

steps.name: Re-prime and repump the interrupted stage
steps.description: After the stoppage the crew primes the pumps, re-pressures the lines and repumps the interrupted stage from pad, or finishes it with a modified ramp agreed with the wellsite supervisor.

evidence.note: Estimate.

steps.name: Hand over to the next shift supervisor
steps.description: The outgoing supervisor walks the incoming one through stages done, pump issues, truck schedule and any open problem with the customer, and writes the handover in the shift log.

evidence.note: Estimate (this well's share of two shift handovers a day).

steps.name: Write the daily operations report
steps.description: Each morning the supervisor writes the daily report for the operations manager and the customer: stages pumped, volumes, pumping hours, downtime by cause and plans for the next 24 hours, copied from the data van summaries and the shift log into a spreadsheet template.

error.defect_description: Volumes or hours are copied wrongly.

evidence.note: Common practice; per-well share estimated.

steps.name: Enter volumes, fuel and pump hours for the field ticket
steps.description: The supervisor keys proppant by mesh, fluid and chemical volumes, pump hours, fuel used and any standby hours into the tablet field ticket, from the data van summary, tote counts and fuel tickets.

error.defect_description: A volume, pump hour or standby line is keyed wrongly.

evidence.note: Re-keying from data van to field ticket was usual in 2019-2022; error rate estimated.

steps.name: Reconcile pumped volumes with the design and tickets
steps.description: The treater compares proppant, fluid and chemical totals in the data van with the field ticket lines, the sand operator's storage drawdown and the design, and sends back any line that does not match.

evidence.note: Estimate.

steps.name: Export treatment data files to the job folder
steps.description: The data technician exports the well's raw data, stage summaries and charts from the acquisition system and copies them to the job folder on the document server, which feeds post-job reporting and the field ticket.

error.defect_description: A file is missing or named for the wrong well.

evidence.note: Estimate.

steps.name: Tell the customer and the coordinator the well is complete
steps.description: The treater emails the wellsite supervisor and the frac operations coordinator that the well's last stage is pumped, with the final totals. For the last well on the pad this also starts rig-down and the move to the next pad.

next.condition: more wells remain on the pad

evidence.note: About three wells per pad as in the organisation file.

exceptions.name: Screen-out
exceptions.description: A stage stops taking proppant; the crew flushes and waits for flowback or a coiled tubing cleanout before repumping.

exceptions.name: Pump or blender failure
exceptions.description: A unit fails and is swapped; four in ten stop the stage.

exceptions.name: Supply or wireline standby
exceptions.description: Sand, water, fuel or wireline is not ready and the fleet stands by.

exceptions.name: Weather hold
exceptions.description: Cold, lightning or storms stop work.

exceptions.name: Incident, spill or offset-well communication
exceptions.description: Pumping stops for a safety or environmental event that must be reported.

exceptions.name: Field ticket correction
exceptions.description: Reconciliation finds a wrongly keyed line.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days attributable to one well, from release of the well to completion notice (fleet time plus the reporting tail)

evidence.note: Derived, not published: about 2,250 tonnes per well (organisation file proppant over wells) at about 1,040 tonnes per operating day (STEP Canada 2021) gives about 2.2 operating days of fleet time, plus about half a day for stoppages and for reconciling and reporting the well after its last stage; p90 adds longer stoppages.

benchmarks.population: STEP Canada frac pads, Q4 2018 to 2019

benchmarks.unit: stages per day on a pad

evidence.note: Midpoints of 3.5-4 and 6-8.

pain_points.description: The fleet and crew sit idle between stages while wireline perforates; zipper fracturing hides most but not all of it.

evidence.note: 2-3 hours per stage on single wells versus about 15 minutes with zipper fracturing.

pain_points.description: Stoppages for screen-outs, pump failures, supplies and weather hold the whole fleet and a crew of about 20 people, worth $3,000 to $5,000 an hour in fleet running cost alone.

evidence.note: Client-location delays and weather cut STEP Canada's Q4 2021 activity; fleet cost per hour from the organisation file.

pain_points.description: Pumping hours per day depend on how well pump maintenance fits into the gaps between stages.

evidence.note: Pumping hours rose from 14-15 to 18-19 a day after maintenance scheduling changes.

pain_points.description: Volumes and pump hours are re-keyed from the data van and paper sheets into the field ticket, and errors surface at reconciliation or in billing disputes.

evidence.note: Common practice before integrated field ticketing; author's estimate of a 8% keying error rate.

sources.title: STEP Energy Services Ltd. Reports Fourth Quarter and Year End 2021 Results
sources.supports: Canadian fracturing 2021: 977 operating days and 1,012,000 tonnes of proppant (about 1,040 tonnes per operating day); 704 days and 776,000 tonnes in 2020; four spreads with 200,000 HP; Q4 2021 work hit by extended delays on a client location from challenging well conditions and by late-December weather; smaller jobs reduce proppant per day; spring break-up restricts equipment moves.

sources.title: Shale Evolution: Zipper Fracture Takes Hold (Trent Jacobs)
sources.supports: Zipper fracturing alternates wells on a pad so wireline perforates one well while another is fractured; six to eight stages a day with zipper versus three and a half to four when each well is done end to end; wireline plug-and-perf between stages normally 2 to 3 hours and up to 5 hours on a single well, down to about 15 minutes of dead time with zipper.

sources.title: Case Study: Increasing Pumping Hours Through Optimized Operations - STEP Energy Services
sources.supports: Canadian frac pads: average pumping hours per day rose from 14.03 (Q4 2018, three pads) to 18.93 on a four-well pad for one client, and from 15.47 (February 2019) to 17.95 (August 2019) for another; gains from managing maintenance schedules, bi-weekly meetings with operators and pre- and post-pad reviews; post-job data delivered to clients through an online tool.

sources.title: Well Site Sand Storage (Sahara)
sources.supports: Wellsite proppant storage unit with 1,800 tonnes of capacity, unloading two trucks at once from any trailer configuration, fully enclosed with dust collection to limit silica exposure, real-time inventory monitoring; record of 6,155 tonnes supplied to the blender in a day.

sources.title: Directive 083: Hydraulic Fracturing - Subsurface Integrity
sources.supports: Directive covers managing subsurface integrity during hydraulic fracturing, including well control at offset wells and protection of nonsaline aquifers; communication events with an offset well are reported on the Hydraulic Fracturing Communication Event Form, events affecting aquifers or water wells and integrity failures with a surface release go to the AER 24-hour response line.

sources.title: Occupations in Alberta: Well Service Equipment Operator
sources.supports: Pumping services use high-pressure pumping equipment and chemicals, fluids or gases; operators monitor control panels and gauges, may mix materials, assemble and connect equipment, work outdoors in all weather, long hours and much travel; tickets include Energy Safety Canada eGSO, WHMIS, H2S, TDG and first aid; pump operators often need a Class 1 licence.

assumptions: Repeated per-stage work (about 28 stages per well, low 12, high 55) is summed into one step per activity, so each step's touch time is the total for the well. This keeps the graph readable and avoids long geometric loops; it means each well takes at most one stoppage branch, which understates the spread of wells with several stoppages.

With zipper fracturing two wells are pumped alternately. The cycle time counts only the fleet time attributable to this well (its pumping, its share of meetings and well-swap dead time), plus the reconciliation and reporting done after its last stage while the next well is pumped; it is not the full calendar span from its first to last stage, which is about the length of the whole pad. The simulated p90 (about 4 days) is below the 4.5-day benchmark because each simulated well takes at most one stoppage.

Concurrent steps s08-s13 are the same pumping hours seen from each role on shift (13 pump operators, 2 blender operators, one sand operator, treater, data technician, supervisor). Labour is touch time times people.

Field staff work 12-hour shifts on a 14-on, 7-off style rotation, about 240 on-site hours a month, not the 130 productive hours the validator's staffing check assumes. Stated FTE is the share of each role's headcount spent on pumping, so it matches the check closely only by coincidence of these two effects.
The frac-pump resource is used only on pump swaps; routine pump running cost is inside the frac-fleet hourly cost so it is not counted twice.

Wells per month (15-50-70) follow the organisation file; with STEP's 1,040 tonnes per operating day, 50 wells a month is consistent with 6-7 crews only if the average well takes about 2,250 tonnes, which matches the organisation file's proppant totals.
Loaded costs come from the organisation file (base wage x 1.35).
